articles.title: Reform says it will prioritise British-born young workers for social housing
articles.summary: Labour called the plan "unserious and unworkable" and accused Reform of pushing "gimmicks and division".
articles.body:
Reform UK has said it will prioritise British-born workers under 35 when allocating social housing if it were to enter government.

On top of British-born workers, former military service personnel and married couples with children will also be prioritised, Reform said.

A Labour spokesperson called the plans "unserious and unworkable", saying it could leave British citizens without a home.

Deputy leader Richard Tice has also set out plans to build 50,000 affordable social homes a year at a news conference, a policy which the party says will require no new taxes or borrowing.

Farage vows to ban foreign nationals from social housing Published 15 June

Farage vows to ban foreign nationals from social housing

Reform plans to scrap indefinite leave to remain for migrants Published 22 September 2025

Reform plans to scrap indefinite leave to remain for migrants

Tice said he wanted the rules on who was allocated a home to be changed away from need to suitability, putting British families, workers and veterans at the front of the queue, saying: "This comes down to fairness."

"We're saying that the first people we should be looking after are young, British workers - under 35, young British married couples, young British veterans - who have done the right thing," he said.

"They've got a job, they're doing their best, working in their community, setting a fine example, because the role of the British government is actually to look after British citizens first."

Rules would be changed to reserve at least half of all social homes in England for British-born workers aged under 35, with prioritisation also given to married couples, veterans, victims of domestic violence and care leavers.

Tice claimed there were currently 540,000 existing affordable social homes occupied by overseas nationals and he wanted that to change.

"It's not fair that young British working families can't get on the housing ladder when overseas nationals have come to the UK and, because of the current rules based on need rather than suitability, they have jumped ahead in the queue," he said.

"We just don't think that's right: I can't think of another country where you rock up with a family and you expect the local taxpayer in that country to pay for your housing needs."

UK or Irish nationals made up 88.5% of main social home householders in 2024/25, according to the English Housing Survey.

That means around 11.5% of main householders, the perÂ­son in whose name the social home is renÂ­ted, were non-UK or Irish nationÂ­als.

For its part, Reform estimates 540,000 social homes are currently occupied by foreign nationals.

Reform has previously announced it would evict foreign nationals from social housing - a plan criticised by housing charity Shelter which said building more homes is the solution, rather than "changing the order of the queue" and "stoking division".

Tice also said Reform would raise Â£10bn a year to build new homes, in part by reintroducing the Right to Buy scheme of the 1980s, allowing people to buy council homes at a discount.

"The failure then was they didn't reinvest the proceeds into building more affordable homes," he said, adding he believed reinvestment would raise a third of the investment needed to build 50,000 homes a year over a decade.

Tice said another third would be raised via housing authorities, and the final third would be money from local government pension schemes.

A Labour Party spokesperson said the plan was "unworkable and unserious", adding: "It would blow a Â£10bn blackhole in the public finances, would create years of wrangling with the EU, and could leave British citizens without a place to call home.

"This Labour government is investing billions to deliver the biggest boost to social and affordable housing in a generation, to fix the housing crisis we inherited from the Tories."

The Conservative Party, which also said it would revoke the right of foreign nationals to social housing, accused Reform of "trying to catch up" with its policies.

The Tories have said their plan, which would allow Irish citizens and some EU nationals to remain in social housing, would free up around 230,000 homes.

Sir James Cleverly, shadow housing secretary, added: "The Conservatives have already set out comprehensive plans to ensure British nationals are at the front of the queue for social housing. Now Reform are trying to catch up.

"We also believe in a home owning society and that those who work hard should be able to buy their own home, without unnecessary barriers standing in their way."

Liberal Democrat spokesperson Gideon Amos said that Reform's plan was a "cruel gimmick".

Green MP SiÃ¢n Berry said her party would tackle housing issues by ending Right to Buy, building and buying hundreds of thousands of new council homes, and introducing rent controls.

She added: "Another blatantly racist and cruel policy from Reform, adding to a host of plans to create a two-tier Britain â one for those born in the UK and one for everyone else."

articles.title: Sullivan endorses Sullivan against Sullivan in Alaska
articles.summary: Three Dan Sullivans are wading in on Alaska’s Senate race but only one Dan Sullivan has earned the support of a former lawmaker with his namesake. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R-Alaska) was endorsed by former Anchorage Mayor Dan A. Sullivan (R) last Tuesday as he prepares to face off against Dan J. Sullivan and Rep.…
articles.body:
Three Dan Sullivans are wading in on Alaska’s Senate race but only one Dan Sullivan has earned the support of a former lawmaker with his namesake.

Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R-Alaska) was endorsed by former Anchorage Mayor Dan A. Sullivan (R) last Tuesday as he prepares to face off against Dan J. Sullivan and Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) in November.

“As the OG Dan Sullivan, I urge Alaskans to vote for Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan. He’s been great for Alaska,” the former mayor of Anchorage wrote in a Facebook post last week.

The post comes after Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign faced legal challenges , as Dan S. Sullivan and the National Republican Senatorial Committee accused him of launching a Senate bid to create confusion for voters seeking to elect the incumbent lawmaker.

Carol Beecher, a registered Republican and the director of the Alaska Division of Elections, attempted to remove Dan J. Sullivan from the primary ballot and disqualify his campaign, citing his logo’s similarities to the incumbent senator’s.

However, Dan J. Sullivan challenged the measure in court, and in June, Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews ruled that Dan J. Sullivan could remain on the ballot for the state’s primary on Aug. 18.

Republicans Dan J. Sullivan and Dan S. Sullivan advanced to Alaska’s general nonpartisan election in November alongside Democrat Peltola (Alaska), who Dan. J. Sullivan has said he voted for twice in previous elections.

The race is considered a toss-up by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report while Decision Desk HQ has Peltola favored to win due to her past success in statewide races and status as a moderate Democrat who hires Republican staffers on the Hill.

Some Republicans have accused Dan J. Sullivan of being a Democratic plant and entering the race to siphon votes away from the incumbent senator with the same name.

Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, has denied those accusations.

articles.title: Bernie Moreno says Natalie Harp discourse has been ‘super misogynistic’
articles.summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) on Sunday said discussions regarding White House aide Natalie Harp in recent days have been “super misogynistic.” Democrats and former White House staffers have said Harp’s relationship with President Trump has been inappropriate, citing reporting from The Daily Beast that unveiled letters to Trump in which she professes her allegiance to…
articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) on Sunday said discussions regarding White House aide Natalie Harp in recent days have been “super misogynistic.”

Democrats and former White House staffers have said Harp’s relationship with President Trump has been inappropriate, citing reporting from The Daily Beast that unveiled letters to Trump in which she professes her allegiance to him.

“You are all that matters to me,” Harp wrote to Trump in one letter. “I don’t want to ever let you down.”

In a separate letter, she wrote, “And please, when I fail, will you tell me? You have the absolute right to cuss me out, if need be, when I deserve it, because no one knows or cares about me more.”

In response to comments alleging an inappropriate relationship between Harp and the president, Moreno told reporters , “That’s super misogynistic.”

“I mean, the reality is she’s a very talented person. She’s very smart at what she does. She helps the president make sure he’s communicating. And the fact that if it was a guy, nobody would say that,” he added.

Moreno said rumors are arising because Harp is “a woman” and “obviously … pretty.”

“When the reality is she’s very talented, she’s very, very smart. I happen to know her very well. It’s also obviously a very kind person. She went through bone cancer in her 20s,” Moreno said.

“I mean, look at the other day, I’ve always said, let’s just keep personal issues out,” he added.

Harp is affectionately referred to as the “human printer” in the White House and is often seen at Trump’s side on Air Force One flights and high-level meetings to provide news clippings and comments for the president on demand.

She campaigned for him in 2024 after she credited Trump for saving her life by signing the Right to Try Act, which gave her access to medical treatments that cured her of cancer.

Following the campaign, Harp transitioned from a television host on One America News Network to a key West Wing aide and executive assistant to the president.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) recently said Trump “doesn’t want to do the job” of president and would rather focus on the White House ballroom project and “travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.” Ossoff made the comments during a campaign rally two weeks ago, referring to the newer Air Force One jet , causing pushback from the White House.

Eric Trump also stepped in to defend Harp , writing, “Natalie is an incredible young woman — a cancer survivor, a genuinely good person, and arguably one of the hardest-working people in the White House. She’s deeply committed to my father, to her job, and to this country,” in a post on the social platform X.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: ministro da Fazenda defende combater 'pejotização' para conter déficit da Previdência Social | G1
articles.standfirst: Durigan falou novamente como representante da campanha à reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, que busca um quarto mandato. Segundo ele, há estudos que mostram que algumas empresas tiveram uma migração de empregados celetistas para pessoa jurídica.
articles.summary: Durigan falou novamente como representante da campanha à reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, que busca um quarto mandato. Segundo ele, há estudos que mostram que algumas empresas tiveram uma migração de empregados celetistas para pessoa jurídica.
articles.body:
O ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, defendeu nesta segunda-feira (24) o combate à chamada "pejotização" como forma de combater o crescente rombo na Previdência Social.

🔎 A "pejotização" é uma contratação sistemática de trabalhadores como pessoas jurídicas (PJ), e não como empregados com carteira assinada. O modelo é legal em diversas atividades, mas gera controvérsia quando é usado para substituir vínculos formais de trabalho previstos na legislação trabalhista.

Em entrevista à Broadcast, da Agência Estado, Durigan falou novamente como representante da campanha à reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) — que busca um quarto mandato.

De acordo com o ministro, há estudos que mostram que algumas empresas tiveram uma migração de empregados celetistas para "pejotizados", o que estaria gerando uma piora no déficit da Previdência Social.

Esses empregados podem, por exemplo, estar sendo contratados como microempreendedores, que têm contribuição reduzida.

"Poderia se ter uma regra no país de uma porcentagem do que uma empresa contrata como pejotizado ou não. Se tem 10% [contratado como pejotizado], está terceirizando um serviço e que é da regra do jogo, é ok. Agora uma empresa que tem 80% da sua força de trabalho pejotizada, eventualmente pode ter de obrigar essa empresa a ter uma contribuição previdenciária para nivelar e poder oferecer aos seus trabalhadores um futuro um pouco mais protegido do ponto de vista da seguridade social", explicou o ministro Durigan.

Ele afirmou que esse tipo de regra tem sido estudada pela equipe econômica, e pode ser apresentada ao Congresso Nacional em um novo mandato do presidente Lula.

"A gente já fez alguns debates nesse sentido", acrescentou o ministro da Fazenda.

Esse tema já havia sido comentado também pelo ministro do Trabalho, Luiz Marinho. No fim de junho, ele disse que o MEI não pode ser utilizado para fraudes trabalhistas e que o micrompreendedor não pode ter características de trabalhadores com carteira assinada.

Na ocasião, o ministro afirmou que há situações em que isso aconteceria – ele cita como exemplo o caso de um hospital que fizesse uma licitação para terceirização de alguma atividade e a empresa terceirizada contratasse MEIs como funcionários formais.

Segundo o ministro, isso poderia "arrebentar" recursos como com a Previdência, o Fundo de Garantia por Tempo de Serviço (FGTS) e o Sistema S, que reúne instituições como Senai, Sesi e Senac.

Marinho disse esperar que o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), que julga ação sobre pejotização na economia , não permita que isso aconteça.

"Não podemos é utilizar o MEI como uma fraude trabalhista, precisa ser empreendedor. Não é o enfermeiro, não é o gari. Isso é fraude trabalhista, não é o gerente. O conceito de debate do que é PJ e não precisa ficar claro, o Supremo tem a responsabilidade de não cometer a irresponsabilidade de permitir contratar PJ como empreendedor. Tem que caracterizar o que é empreendedor", disse Marinho a jornalistas, em junho.

Ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan — Foto: Washington Costa/MF

articles.title: Ancine concede registro a 'Dark Horse', cinebiografia de Jair Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Concessão do Registro de Obra Estrangeira (ROE) é etapa preliminar ao registro definitivo da obra. Em paralelo, agência apura irregularidade na gravação do filme.
articles.summary: Concessão do Registro de Obra Estrangeira (ROE) é etapa preliminar ao registro definitivo da obra. Em paralelo, agência apura irregularidade na gravação do filme.
articles.body:
A Agência Nacional do Cinema (Ancine) concedeu o Registro de Obra Estrangeira (ROE) de Dark Horse, filme sobre a trajetória do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL).

O pedido, aceito no dia 7 de agosto, é uma etapa preliminar ao registro definitivo da obra ( veja os próximos passos abaixo ).

🎥O filme "Dark Horse" ganhou notoriedade após a divulgação, pelo site Intercept Brasil, de conversas entre o pré-candidato do PL à Presidência, Flávio Bolsonaro, e o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, do banco Master, em que o filho de Jair solicita recursos para financiar a produção cinematográfica.

O filme, protagonizado pelo ator norte-americano Jim Caviezel no papel de Jair Bolsonaro, terá 1h40 de duração e é classificada pela Ancine como uma obra de ficção.

A concessão do registro ocorre ao mesmo tempo que a Ancine abriu um processo administrativo contra a produtora responsável pelo filme, a Go Up Entertainment .

O processo foi aberto após uma denúncia sobre a gravação, em território brasileiro, de uma obra audiovisual estrangeira sem comunicação prévia à agência.

Pela regulamentação, produções estrangeiras filmadas no Brasil precisam informar previamente a Ancine e apresentar documentos sobre a produção.

Além disso, na semana passada, a Polícia Federal solicitou à Ancine informações sobre o processo aberto contra o filme . Segundo a Ancine, a Go Up não havia apresentado a documentação exigida para as gravações.

A empresa pode ser multada em R$ 2 mil a R$ 100 mil caso a irregularidade seja confirmada.

Jim Caviezel no pôster de 'Dark Horse' — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram/therealjimcaviezel

O pedido da PF ocorre em paralelo à investigação sobre o financiamento do filme. O Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) autorizou, em julho deste ano, a abertura de um inquérito para apurar os repasses feitos pelo empresário Daniel Vorcaro, ex-controlador do Banco Master, para a produção.

A investigação busca verificar se os recursos foram efetivamente utilizados para financiar Dark Horse.

LEIA TAMBÉM: 'Dark Horse': entenda o que a PF vai investigar sobre a cinebiografia de Jair Bolsonaro

A origem do caso está em mensagens e áudios que indicam que o candidato à Presidência, Flávio Bolsonaro (PF), teria pedido dinheiro a Vorcaro para financiar o filme.

O valor inicialmente mencionado nas negociações chegou a US$ 24 milhões (cerca de R$ 134 milhões), embora os valores efetivamente transferidos sejam objeto da investigação.

Após obter o registro, o responsável pela obra deverá solicitar o Certificado de Registro de Título (CRT), indicando o segmento de mercado em que a obra será explorada.

No caso de um filme destinado à exibição comercial em cinemas, como é o de "Dark Horse", o segmento correspondente é o de salas de exibição.

Para a emissão do CRT, deve ser demonstrada a detenção dos direitos de exploração comercial da obra no Brasil e para o segmento pretendido, mediante a apresentação do contrato de cessão, licenciamento ou transferência desses direitos.

Registro de Obra Estrangeira (ROE) de "Dark Horse", filme sobre Jair Bolsonaro — Foto: Reprodução

Quando houver uma cadeia de contratos, como nos casos que envolvem produtor estrangeiro, agente internacional de vendas e distribuidor brasileiro, a documentação deve permitir verificar a transferência dos direitos até o responsável pela exploração comercial no Brasil.

O certificado, portanto, está vinculado à etapa de exploração comercial da obra e não representa uma exigência para a realização das filmagens.

A conclusão do procedimento de registro depende do atendimento das eventuais exigências e diligências formuladas pela Ancine. Os procedimentos regulamentares de registro têm prazo de até 30 dias para conclusão quando não houver exigências a serem cumpridas.

Após a emissão do CRT é necessário ainda a obtenção da classificação indicativa no Ministério da Justiça, para depois lançar comercialmente o filme nas salas de cinema.

A obra só poderá ser lançada comercialmente após o cumprimento de todas as etapas.

articles.title: Romeu Zema em entrevista à Globo: salário mínimo e aposentadoria  | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do Novo foi o primeiro a participar da série de entrevistas ao vivo da Globo com os presidenciáveis das eleições 2026.
articles.summary: Em entrevista à Globo, o candidato Romeu Zema vinculou o reajuste do salário mínimo ao crescimento econômico e comentou possíveis mudanças na Previdência.
articles.body:
O candidato do Novo à Presidência da República, Romeu Zema, afirmou nesta segunda-feira (24), em entrevista à Globo, que, se eleito, garantirá a reposição da inflação no salário mínimo, mas não se comprometeu com aumento real. Segundo ele, reajustes acima da inflação dependerão do desempenho da economia.

O ex-governador ainda disse que manteria o ganho com relação ao crescimento dos dois anos anteriores se a economia “estiver indo bem”.

Zema propõe ajuste fiscal para baixar juros a 6%, sem detalhar medidas, e defende anistia para condenados do 8 de janeiro

Zema disse que a prioridade dele, se eleito, é que a taxa de juros caia. “Com um governo sério, com credibilidade, combatendo corrupção e fraudes, essa taxa cai para 6%. Só aí nós vamos ter uma economia de R$ 800 bilhões por ano”.

Zema afirmou ainda que, “por ora”, não pretende aumentar as idades mínimas para aposentadoria. O candidato, porém, não descartou mudanças futuras e disse que eventuais alterações nas regras da Previdência dependerão de fatores como o aumento da expectativa de vida da população e uma maior formalização do mercado de trabalho.

Questionado sobre possíveis mudanças nas regras para trabalhadores rurais e militares, Zema também condicionou decisões ao resultado do ajuste fiscal que pretende implementar caso seja eleito.

articles.title: Discord recorre de suspensão de lives e diz que ANPD aplicou punição 'desproporcional' à plataforma | G1
articles.standfirst: Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados suspendeu transmissões da plataforma até que o Discord comprove que adotou medidas para proteger menores. Em julho, adolescente se suicidou durante live.
articles.summary: Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados suspendeu transmissões da plataforma até que o Discord comprove que adotou medidas para proteger menores. Em julho, adolescente se suicidou durante live.
articles.body:
O Discord apresentou nesta segunda-feira (24) um recurso contra a suspensão de lives da plataforma determinada pela Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD).

A empresa solicita efeito suspensivo imediato com o objetivo de reativar as transmissões e pede a anulação da medida cautelar, alegando falta de competência da agência para aplicar a restrição, vícios formais no processo e punição "desproporcional".

🔎 O debate sobre a segurança no ambiente digital ganhou força nas últimas semanas após a primeira-dama, Janja da Silva, dizer que o Discord deveria ser retirado do ar “imediatamente” , ao se referir a uma adolescente que tirou a própria vida durante transmissões em grupos da plataforma .

💻 O Discord é uma plataforma de comunicação bastante utilizada por jogadores de games online e também por adolescentes. A empresa tem sido alvo de críticas e investigações relacionadas a falhas na moderação de conteúdo e na verificação da idade dos usuários.

A ordem de suspensão atingiu a ferramenta "Go Live" e recursos equivalentes de transmissão e compartilhamento de vídeo. A determinação foi cumprida pelo Discord em 17 de agosto .

🔎 A ANPD é uma agência reguladora vinculada ao Ministério da Justiça , cuja missão é zelar pela proteção de dados pessoais.

Segundo a ANPD, a suspensão valerá até que o Discord comprove que adotou medidas efetivas para proteger crianças e adolescentes durante o uso da plataforma.

Punição atinge quem não tem elo com ilícitos, diz defesa

No recurso protocolado, a plataforma diz que a ANPD não tem competência legal para determinar a suspensão de serviços sob o marco do ECA Digital.

A defesa do Discord afirma que a lei estabelece que sanções como advertência e multa cabem à autoridade administrativa, mas a suspensão temporária ou proibição de atividades é atribuição da justiça.

A defesa também declara que, mesmo dentro da esfera administrativa, uma medida de tamanho impacto e alcance nacional não poderia ter sido emitida monocraticamente pelo Superintendente de Fiscalização.

O recurso do Discord afirma ainda que o bloqueio das chamadas de vídeo em grupo e transmissões privadas afeta diariamente famílias, estudantes, comunidades e empresas em todo o Brasil que nada têm a ver com condutas ilícitas.

Caso a suspensão das lives não seja integralmente anulada ou reconsiderada pela Superintendência, o Discord pede o envio do processo ao Conselho Diretor da ANPD.

A conversão da suspensão em um Plano de Conformidade, com cronograma técnico de entregas e metas claras;

A fixação imediata de prazo e critérios objetivos para a reativação faseada dos serviços;

O prosseguimento das discussões institucionais e a formalização de um Termo de Ajustamento de Conduta (TAC) centralizado na autoridade.

Depois de live que terminou em morte, Discord suspende transmissões ao vivo no país — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

articles.title: Romeu Zema (Novo), candidato à Presidência, concede entrevista à Globo | G1
articles.standfirst: Os jornalistas Renata Vasconcellos e César Tralli conduziram a primeira entrevista da série da Globo com os candidatos à Presidência da República, direto dos Estúdios Globo, no Rio de Janeiro.
articles.summary: Romeu Zema abre a rodada de conversas com presidenciáveis sob o comando de Renata Vasconcellos e César Tralli, com transmissão ao vivo no g1 e GloboNews.
articles.body:
O candidato do Novo à Presidência da República, Romeu Zema , afirmou nesta segunda-feira (24) que, se eleito, vai promover medidas de ajuste fiscal para que a taxa básica de juros, a Selic, caia a 6% ao ano. Atualmente, a Selic está em 14% ao ano .

LEIA TAMBÉM: Zema não garante aumento real do salário mínimo e diz que, 'por ora', não mexeria em idades de aposentadoria

Zema não detalhou, no entanto, em que consistiria esse ajuste fiscal ou como faria para obter a redução na taxa de juros.

O candidato disse ainda que, se eleito, vai garantir que o salário mínimo seja reajustado pela inflação. “Garanto que ninguém vai ter perda”, disse o ex-governador de Minas Gerais. Um reajuste com ganho real, porém, estaria condicionado ao bom desempenho da economia, disse.

LEIA TAMBÉM: Veja o que é #FATO e o que é #FAKE na entrevista de Romeu Zema à Globo

Zema concedeu nesta segunda-feira (24) entrevista à Globo. A atração foi exibida ao vivo dos Estúdios Globo, no Rio de Janeiro, com transmissão pelo g1 e pela GloboNews. Ao longo desta semana, até sábado, serão entrevistados os candidatos Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), Renan Santos (Missão), Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Augusto Cury (Avante).

Romeu Zema, candidato à Presidência da República pelo Novo — Foto: Globo/ Manoella Mello

Veja destaques da entrevista de Romeu Zema à Globo:

Ao falar sobre propostas de ajuste fiscal, Zema disse que, se eleito, garantirá a reposição da inflação no salário mínimo.

“Garanto que ninguém vai ter perda”, declarou. “Se tiver inflação, nós daremos toda a inflação. É um absurdo um aposentado não ter a reposição inflacionária ou, pior, ficar sem receber a aposentadoria”.

O ex-governador ainda disse que manteria o ganho com relação ao crescimento dos dois anos anteriores se a economia “estiver indo bem”.

Zema disse que a prioridade dele, se eleito, é que a taxa de juros caia. “Com um governo sério, com credibilidade, combatendo corrupção e fraudes, essa taxa cai para 6%. Só aí nós vamos ter uma economia de R$ 800 bilhões por ano”.

A primeira pergunta a Zema foi sobre como ele pretende, se eleito, equilibrar os gastos do país, dado que, enquanto governador de Minas Gerais, a dívida pública do estado praticamente dobrou. Segundo ele, isso aconteceu porque o déficit foi “herdado dos anos 90” e porque o governo federal cobrava juros altos.

Zema afirmou que não fez nenhum empréstimo ou financiamento durante sua gestão de quase 8 anos em Minas.

“Eu paguei R$ 23 bilhões para aposentado que não recebia aposentadoria”, disse. “Eu paguei R$ 13 bilhões para o governo federal, funcionários públicos, e hoje a dívida representa muito menos para a economia de Minas do que representava quando eu assumi.”

Ainda de acordo com o candidato, ele assumiu com um déficit de R$ 11 bilhões em 2018 e deixou o cargo com um superávit de R$ 5 bilhões. “Ou seja, o estado gastando menos do que arrecada, e antes gastava-se muito mais do que arrecadava. O ajuste foi feito.”

Zema foi questionado sobre seu posicionamento contrário à vacinação obrigatória de crianças. O Estado de São Paulo enfrenta um surto de sarampo. O candidato concorda que situações como esta colocam em risco a sociedade como um todo.

“Eu tomei todas as vacinas da Covid, acredito na ciência, recomendo que tome. Em Minas, eu recomendei que as crianças tomassem”, disse. “Agora, eu não posso permitir que uma família, uma criança seja perseguida porque alguém não tomou a vacina."

Para o candidato, o papel do governo é fazer campanha de conscientização e vacinar o maior número de pessoas possível. Segundo ele, a obrigatoriedade não pode ser imposta em “um país democrático”.

O candidato disse que, se eleito presidente, dará anistia aos condenados pelos atos golpistas de 8 de janeiro de 2023 e classificou o julgamento dessas pessoas, feito pelo STF, como “nitidamente político”.

Segundo Zema, os responsáveis devem ser punidos por vandalismo e depredação. Na avaliação dele, há tribunais no Brasil “fazendo mais política do que propriamente justiça”.

“Eu darei anistia ou, pelo menos, no mínimo, um tribunal que não seja político, um tribunal que seja judicial”, disse.

Zema também afirmou confiar nas urnas eletrônicas, embora defenda que o sistema poderia ser “melhorado” com voto impresso.

"Vale lembrar: eu sou totalmente democrata, fui eleito pela urna eletrônica, confio na urna eletrônica — que poderia ser melhorada se tivesse impresso, mas confio."

Zema afirmou que medidas adotadas pelo governo de Nayib Bukele, presidente de El Salvador, para reduzir os homicídios podem ser adaptadas ao Brasil. O candidato visitou o país em maio de 2025 para conhecer a política de segurança pública.

Questionado especificamente sobre medidas do governo Bukele, como suspensão de direitos, Zema disse que não concorda, mas disse que o exemplo salvadorenho o inspira por ter colocado criminosos “atrás das grades” e reduzido os homicídios. “Será que não é isso que nós queremos aqui? Nós podemos fazer prisões aqui dentro da nossa lei”, afirmou.

Questionado sobre como combateria a violência contra as mulheres, o candidato citou a ampliação do número de delegacias especializadas no atendimento à mulher, com atendimento feito por funcionárias femininas, e de casas de acolhimento para vítimas de violência doméstica.

Também mencionou o uso de recursos tecnológicos, como tornozeleiras eletrônicas com distância mínima de 200 metros da vítima e possibilidade de chamar automaticamente a polícia. Disse, ainda, que o aspecto mais importante é a conscientização nas escolas. “Toda criança deve ser conscientizada de que, caso tenha violência em casa, precisa considerar isso anormal”.

Em seguida, Zema foi questionado sobre o aumento do número de feminicídios registrados em Minas Gerais em 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 e 2025, durante o governo dele.

“Quando eu assumi, eu sempre pego a estatística antes do meu governo e no meu governo. E eu posso te assegurar que nós reduzimos. Algum repique sempre pode acontecer”, respondeu. “Agora, o que vale é a tendência ao longo do tempo. Mas todas as medidas, todos esses planos foram feitos em Minas. Vale lembrar, tem uma taxa menor do que a média.”

Ao ser questionado sobre a promessa de privatizar estatais federais se for eleito presidente, apesar de não ter conseguido vender a Cemig, principal empresa estatal mineira quando foi governador, Zema afirmou que vendeu 118 empresas e participações do governo de Minas Gerais durante os anos em que esteve à frente do estado.

O ex-governador citou entre os ativos negociados participações na Light e na Companhia Brasileira de Lítio, além da privatização da Copasa. Segundo ele, uma mudança na Constituição mineira exigia o apoio de três quintos da Assembleia Legislativa para a venda de estatais e essa maioria foi alcançada no caso da companhia de saneamento.

“Ficou faltando uma empresa só. Todas as outras foram vendidas. E, lembrando um detalhe importantíssimo durante a minha gestão, a empresa de saneamento de Minas, que é a Copasa, e a empresa de energia de Minas, que é a Cemig valorizaram estrondosos 300%, porque não teve roubalheira, não teve corrupção. Foi uma gestão profissional, valorizando o patrimônio do mineiro, e eu vou fazer o mesmo no Brasil”, disse o candidato.

Zema afirmou que não pretende, inicialmente, aumentar a idade mínima para aposentadoria. Segundo o candidato, eventuais mudanças na Previdência dependerão também do aumento da expectativa de vida da população e de uma maior formalização no mercado de trabalho.

Questionado sobre possíveis alterações nas regras para trabalhadores rurais e militares, Zema afirmou que as decisões dependerão do resultado do ajuste fiscal que pretende implementar, se eleito. O candidato disse que pretende reduzir gastos, combater fraudes e corrupção e melhorar a eficiência da administração pública.

“A aposentadoria vai depender muito disso. Agora, o brasileiro já trabalha muito. Eu não quero o brasileiro trabalhando mais. Eu quero a renda do brasileiro aumentando”, afirmou Zema.

O candidato à Presidência prometeu aumentar em dez vezes o número de escolas de tempo integral no país. Segundo ele, a meta de longo prazo é universalizar o modelo.

Zema citou sua gestão como governador e afirmou que o número de escolas com ensino médio em tempo integral passou de cerca de 70, quando assumiu o governo, para mais de 800 ao deixar o cargo.

“Me comprometo, como eu fiz em Minas, dez vezes. Dez vezes”, afirmou ao ser questionado sobre qual seria sua meta para os quatro anos de mandato. “Países desenvolvidos, países sérios, a criança fica na escola o dia todo."

Zema foi questionado sobre a redução de investimento em informação e inteligência de R$ 533 milhões para R$ 200 milhões no estado de Minas Gerais durante a sua gestão. Segundo o Anuário Brasileiro de Segurança Pública. Respondeu que o governo foi marcado por quedas contínuas na criminalidade.

O ex-governador disse que considera a rubrica importante, e que, durante a realização de levantamentos de informação, o investimento pode “cair numa outra sigla e não ser considerado”. Como exemplo, citou uma comparação entre a compra de viaturas e serviços de inteligência.

Ainda segundo Zema, os investimentos em segurança pública em Minas Gerais cresceram ao longo do seu governo. “Tem outra questão também: quem constrói uma casa neste ano, no ano que vem a despesa com construção diminui. Talvez a implantação tenha sido no início do meu governo e depois foram manutenções”, argumentou. “Enquanto a despesa foi alta, você estava adquirindo o sistema, implantando — é lógico que ela vai cair depois. Mas o que interessa é o resultado.”

Outra pergunta foi sobre a Operação Rejeito, ação da Polícia Federal deflagrada durante o governo do candidato, que identificou uma organização criminosa que atuou para obter vantagens econômicas por meio de crimes ambientais, lavagem de dinheiro e corrupção.

“Fica aqui o meu repúdio a esses bandidos que, além de estarem recebendo dinheiro, estavam destruindo o meio ambiente”, afirmou. “Quero que tudo seja apurado e que esses bandidos mofem na prisão."

Na avaliação de Zema, um estado com mais de 300 mil funcionários está sujeito a ter “algumas frutas podres”. Ele afirmou que seu governo tomou “todas as medidas”, defendendo “investigação, polícia, prisão, [e] punição”.

Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro, Renan Santos, Ronaldo Caiado, Augusto Cury e Romeu Zema: candidatos à Presidência da República — Foto: Divulgação

Romeu Zema, de 61 anos, é empresário e ex-governador de Minas Gerais. Depois de se afastar da gestão das empresas da família para entrar na política, foi eleito governador em 2018 e reeleito em 2022. Agora, candidato do Novo à Presidência, tenta se apresentar como uma alternativa ao bolsonarismo, embora tenha apoiado Jair Bolsonaro nas duas eleições anteriores. Leia o perfil do candidato.

Zema se aproximou da família Bolsonaro em 2018, mas passou a se distanciar e, mais recentemente, intensificou as críticas a Flávio Bolsonaro, dizendo que é preciso unir a direita para derrotar Lula. Nas pesquisas, aparecia com 2% das intenções de voto na Quaest de 14 de agosto.

Romeu Zema, César Tralli e Renata Vasconcellos nos Estúdios Globo, no Rio de Janeiro — Foto: Globo/ Manoella Mello

O discurso de Zema mantém como eixos a redução do tamanho do Estado, reformas administrativas e críticas ao PT e ao STF. Zema defende mudanças nas regras para ministros da Corte e já entrou em conflito público com Gilmar Mendes.

No governo de Minas, das 12 promessas feitas em 2022, quatro foram cumpridas integralmente , cinco parcialmente e três não foram cumpridas.

O plano de governo de Romeu Zema para a Presidência, registrado no TSE , propõe uma agenda de forte redução da participação do Estado na economia, flexibilização das relações trabalhistas e endurecimento das políticas de segurança pública.

Entre as medidas estão a privatização de estatais, mudanças na Previdência e na CLT, ampliação do acesso a armas, redução da maioridade penal, mudanças no funcionamento do STF e alterações no sistema político e na política externa.

Veja as principais propostas de Zema, registradas no TSE:

permitir o porte de armas em toda a extensão das propriedades rurais;

classificar facções criminosas como organizações terroristas e empregar as Forças Armadas na retomada de territórios;

privatizar todas as empresas estatais e ampliar parcerias público-privadas, inclusive em saúde e educação;

criar um regime de contratação alternativo à CLT;

depositar R$ 1 mil para cada brasileiro ao nascer - o dinheiro seria aplicado em fundos de ações e retirado quando o beneficiário completasse 18 anos;

reduzir a maioridade penal para 16 anos, com possibilidade de responsabilização de pessoas ainda mais jovens em casos excepcionais;

internar involuntariamente, ou seja, mesmo contra a vontade da pessoa, dependentes de drogas e álcool que vivem nas ruas;

proibir barracas e abrigos improvisados em calçadas, praças e outros espaços públicos;

criar um programa nacional para estimular a união progressiva de municípios sem sustentação financeira própria;

acabar com os fundos Eleitoral e Partidário;

retirar o Brasil do Brics e buscar a entrada na Organização para a Cooperação e Desenvolvimento Econômico (OCDE).

articles.title: Dan Sullivan endorses Dan Sullivan to beat Dan Sullivan in perplexing Alaska Senate race
articles.summary: A third Dan Sullivan — a former Anchorage mayor — has weighed in on the competitive Senate race, endorsing Sen. Dan S. Sullivan over former teacher Dan J. Sullivan.
articles.body: A new Dan Sullivan has entered the conversation surrounding the Alaska Senate race, in which incumbent Dan S. Sullivan faces a candidate with the same name. The Republican former mayor of Anchorage, Dan A. Sullivan, endorsed GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan for re-election over retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan and Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola on Tuesday. “As the OG Dan Sullivan, I urge Alaskans to vote for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. He’s been great for Alaska,” the former mayor wrote on Facebook. Both Dan S. Sullivan and Peltola advanced to the general election in November after the all-party primary last week, in which the top four finishers advance, regardless of political affiliation. NBC News has not yet made a call regarding who the other two candidates will be, but Dan J. Sullivan could be among them. Alaska’s Senate race is considered one of the most competitive this cycle, when control of the upper chamber hangs in the balance. With primary votes left to count, Peltola so far has 48% of the vote, with Sen. Dan S. Sullivan taking 43%. Dan J. Sullivan — who is running as a Republican — has 2.4%, with other candidates getting considerably fewer votes. The general election for the Senate race will be decided by ranked-choice voting. Democrats view the election as a seat they could flip in November. The Cook Political Report rates the race a toss-up. The Sullivan saga has drawn attention as former teacher Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy has faced legal challenges. Dan S. Sullivan and Republicans have alleged that the teacher was placed on the ballot to confuse voters and detract from the senator’s share of the vote, claiming he’s working with Peltola. Dan J. Sullivan has denied coordinating with the Peltola campaign. Peltola has also denied any involvement with the second Sullivan campaign. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled last month that Dan J. Sullivan can stay on the ballot after the state Division of Elections originally disqualified him. NBC News has reported that state and federal prosecutors in Alaska were investigating whether the race could be part of a conspiracy to confuse voters. A grand jury issued subpoenas this month to compel information from witnesses linked to Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign. The state uses ranked-choice voting in the general election, not the primary.

articles.title: This democratic socialist has upset the party establishment. Here’s her strategy for Congress
articles.summary: As the Democratic Party’s socialist summer comes to a close, Darializa Avila Chevalier has become one of the most polarizing — and potentially most influenti...
articles.body:
This August's Dominican Heritage Reception at Gracie Mansion brought in a different crowd from years past.

Dozens of Dominican Americans, including activists more used to protesting than attending the event, mingled over trays of cheese empanadas and sancocho. Dressed in a butter yellow guayabera, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani took a moment to shout out the notable community members in the crowd. The longest, loudest applause went to Darializa Avila Chevalier, the 32-year-old democratic socialist who defeated the chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus in June's Democratic primary.

Such friendly audiences, she knows, may become a rarity as she braces for Congress.

As the Democratic Party's socialist summer comes to a close, Avila Chevalier has become one of the most polarizing — and potentially most influential — faces of an insurgency that has bested several congressional incumbents and left the party at a crossroads.

Ahead of the midterms, the party is now grappling with the power Avila Chevalier and at least four other democratic socialist nominees could have if Democrats take back the House in November. If House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries wins a single-digit majority, the incoming cohort and its allies on the left could have huge sway over his potential speakership and demand concessions on a host of progressive priorities.

Already, Avila Chevalier and her allies are discussing how they want to lead and how they plan to work together.

"Our movement has worked too hard for me to allow myself to be distracted," Avila Chevalier told CNN. "We've been talking about how do we come in strong on day one, and really, meaningfully build a model of co-governance that gives power back to working people."

Avila Chevalier, a community organizer and doctoral student who centered her campaign on uncompromising support for Palestinians and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, has grown used to the noise surrounding her.

In the final weeks of her primary against Rep. Adriano Espaillat, much was made of her old tweets from a now-deleted account criticizing Democratic leaders and embracing far-left policies, as well as her attendance at a controversial rally in support of Palestinians the day after Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Avila Chevalier has since become a fixture on Fox News, a target of President Donald Trump's rallies, and a source of anxiety for House Democrats worried about being painted as socialists or communists by the GOP.

Progressives have urged party leadership to not fall into what they say is a familiar trap.

"Republicans are always encouraging us to divide ourselves," said Rep. Summer Lee, a progressive Pennsylvania Democrat. "I also see a lot of people who are trying to make her a boogeyman, who are trying to make her a pariah, and I am trying, and I really want to fight back against that instinct."

Similar dynamics played out after the 2018 midterms, when members of what became the "Squad" defeated longtime incumbents and quickly joined protests on Capitol Hill.

Some of those members, such as New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — who did not endorse Avila Chevalier — have shown an ability to work within the caucus and across the aisle on key issues. Others, such as former Reps. Cori Bush of Missouri and Jamaal Bowman of New York, became better known for what they did outside the legislative process, leaving them vulnerable to successful primary challenges.

"It's one thing to be noisy, it's another thing to be intentional, and meaningful, and being able to deliver on the things you promise," said Antjuan Seawright, a Democratic strategist and longtime advisor to South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn.

Avila Chevalier is making the case that she's an organizer who is focused on making her platform a reality. Her challenge now is reintroducing herself to the party establishment she just took on.

"I am very concerned with delivering," she said. "I think folks will be, hopefully, pleasantly surprised about the fact that yes, I am really willing to talk to anybody, literally anybody, who wants to actually deliver for working people."

Avila Chevalier grew up in Florida, with brief stints in New York and Venezuela. Though her maternal grandfather was part of the resistance against dictator Rafael Trujillo back in the Dominican Republic, her family talked about politics in terms of the cost of gas or cuts to benefits. She, however, showed an interest in social justice early on.

Mariangelly Abreu, a distant relative she calls a cousin and who grew up alongside her, said Avila Chevalier would encourage them to buy flowers from the sellers on street corners instead of the supermarket and make other intentional choices about where they spent their money.

"My cousin can be — and I say this with so much love — annoyingly persistent," Abreu said. "She's not someone who will just say, 'Oh, well, that's just how things are.'"

Avila Chevalier applied to Columbia University to find a way to New York. Part of the school's appeal was that it was the "activist Ivy" and she soon joined the Black Student Organization and started organizing to end sexual assault on campus.

In her sophomore year, she came across a posting for a summer internship to teach English to Palestinians living in refugee camps in the West Bank. Her experience there, and the conditions she witnessed, helped shape the organizing work that would define her adult life and inspired her to convert to Islam.

"It was an opportunity for me to really get clear on what my values are, on what it means to advocate for human dignity even when it's politically hard, even when there is so much that is pushing you to stay silent on things," she said.

Some of the highs and lows of her campaign trace back to that trip and the work in which she subsequently engaged. Avila Chevalier became an active member of Students for Justice in Palestine, and returned to Columbia as an alumna to support students as they took over part of the campus in 2024 to protest Israel's military actions in Gaza. There she worked alongside Mahmoud Khalil, a fellow organizer who was later detained by the Trump administration for more than three months.

Avila Chevalier pointed to her West Bank experience to justify her presence at the October 8th rally, held in support of Gaza the day after Hamas attacked Israel, that featured speech and rhetoric praising the attack, in which 1,200 Israelis were killed and 250 more kidnapped. According to reports, pro-Palestinian protesters chanted "from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free" and "resistance is justified, when people are colonized."

Soon after she returned to the US in 2014, Hamas militants kidnapped and killed three Israeli teenagers, triggering a military response from Israel that killed an estimated 2,251 Palestinians. Avila Chevalier said she feared a similar large-scale counter-response in 2023. An estimated 70,000 people have died in Gaza in the war after October 7th.

Asked if there's anything she feels she needs to apologize for regarding the rally, Avila Chevalier said, "There are people who've expressed views in spaces like this who you don't always agree with." But she said she hoped those who attended pro-Israel rallies where some attendees have made inflammatory remarks would also reject those comments.

Avila Chevalier's organizing and academic work on immigration has fueled her belief that ICE must be abolished and that all deportations are wrong. Before running for Congress, she worked with Families for Freedom to try to block deportations and spent three years attending deportation hearings and interviewing people caught up in the process as part of her PhD in sociology at the City University of New York.

Late last year, Avila Chevalier called her adviser, Professor David Brotherton, to say she was being recruited to challenge Espaillat and would be unlikely to complete her dissertation on time if she decided to run.

"I said, 'No, I don't think you probably are,'" he recalled telling her. "If it's a question of making history or writing a dissertation, I would choose the former."

Early last year, Avila Chevalier reached out to Justice Democrats, the same progressive group that recruited Ocasio-Cortez, to see if there was a window for someone to primary Espaillat.

Over his five terms in Congress — and several decades as a state legislator and local political leader — Espaillat had built up a formidable political presence in the district, including local officials he'd mentored known as the "Squadriano." Avila Chevalier and other Espaillat critics argued the congressman was absent from the district.

A spokesperson for Espaillat pushed back on that assessment, noting his work on immigration cases, pandemic recovery and affordable housing. "Soon, campaigning and slogans have to give way to governing and leading," the spokesperson said in a statement.

Those early talks of a challenge lapsed until Mamdani, a democratic socialist, won the district in last year's mayoral primary.

Last August, Geoff Simpson, Justice Democrats' PAC director emailed her about running after local organizers recommended her. It took two and a half months of conversations to convince her to run, he said.

"People like to get plugged in at the end with like the TV ads and the messaging," Simpson said. "But if you get the candidate recruitment piece wrong, none of that ends up mattering."

Ahead of her launch, the group targeted two key and ambitious endorsements: the New York City Democratic Socialists of America, which was wading into congressional races for the first time, and Mamdani, who had been endorsed by Espaillat in the mayoral general election.

During an endorsement meeting earlier this year, NYC-DSA co-chair Gustavo Gordillo worried the group wouldn't be able to both challenge Espaillat and back Assemblymember Claire Valdez in the open 7th Congressional District.

"I wasn't sure if we would be able to meet the moment, and I'm really glad that members proved me wrong, and we did," he told CNN.

His support drew attention to the race, as well as her record.

News outlets, including CNN , reported on tweets Avila Chevalier either personally wrote or reposted between 2018 and 2022 on a since-deleted account. Some — including a post that called on people to "become bad bitches" and "seize the means of production" — were written in the flippant, ironic tone favored by far-left online posters. But several made serious calls for defunding and abolishing the police and criticized Israel and Democratic politicians. After former Vice President Kamala Harris made a speech telling Central American migrants "do not come" to the United States, Avila Chevalier tweeted, "F**k Kamala Harris."

Avila Chevalier said she's grown since using that language and regrets her post history. In reflecting on the account, she said she was part of a generation that came of age online.

"We are the first generation to really be forming our sense of self and our political identities and our political worldviews in such a public way, and that inevitably means that we're going to say things that we'll eventually not agree with or feel cringe about or regret," she said.

Avila Chevalier said it was painful to see her deleted tweets become a distraction from the issues she wanted to highlight. At the same time, she said it wasn't lost on her that the words of a 20-something with no political power were being dissected while "we have folks who have been in political power for almost as long as I've been alive, or longer, who have passed policy that have cost people their lives."

"That is at the heart of the problem that we've had for so long, is that accountability feels unreachable in our political system," she said.

It's not clear how the House Democratic Caucus will respond to Avila Chevalier or the other Justice Democrats and DSA-aligned candidates who won blue district primaries this cycle, but early indicators suggest a mix of wariness, defiance and, in some cases, cautious optimism.

Publicly, party leadership has congratulated them. But moderate Democrats are also making a point of spurning socialism to reduce the sting of Republican attacks.

Jeffries said earlier this month on NBC's Meet the Press that he rejects the national Democratic Socialists of America agenda, wants to reform but not abolish ICE and no longer supports Medicare for All after previously co-sponsoring the bill. But he acknowledged the party will have a "broad caucus" in January.

The challenge for Avila Chevalier is that, as of now, there is a perception that she is more of an activist than a coalition builder.

The difference is activism is about calling attention to an issue, said Ilona Duverge, Avila Chevalier's campaign manager. "An organizer," she said, "is going to think of 'What are the steps, what is the path that I need to forge in order to actually meet my goal?'"

Avila Chevalier has three top priorities, what she described on the campaign trail as housing for all, "babies not bombs," and abolishing ICE. Among the 13 bills she's promised to cosponsor on her first day of Congress is Illinois Rep. Delia Ramirez's Block the Bombs Act, which would stop the unconditional transfer of offensive military weapons to Israel. She'll also back the Green New Deal, Medicare for All Act, and legislation to boost unions and raise the federal minimum wage.

Ramirez said she's been vocal with leadership about making sure Avila Chevalier as well as the other far-left primary winners feel welcome in DC. She described the New York candidate as someone who asks questions, "genuinely wants to grow, wants to learn" and wants to fight for the district.

"She also understands she can't come here and spend 20 years here before she can deliver," Ramirez said.

The likely incoming members are also still figuring out how they'll wield their influence in what could be a very narrow House Democratic majority.

"The most important thing is that we're getting into the habit of calling each other when we have questions," said Valdez, the Democratic nominee for the 7th District who is also backed by Mamdani, the DSA and Justice Democrats. "We're still figuring out what the demands will be."

In the meantime, the nominees have been focused on building up their support in their districts. For Avila Chevalier, that's meant meet-and-greets and community events.

Earlier this month she joined New York state Sen. Gustavo Rivera to hand out backpacks and school supplies to a long line of families that wrapped around a park in the South Bronx, a part of the district that heavily favored the incumbent. Rivera, who didn't endorse in the primary but said he voted for Avila Chevalier, introduced the Democratic nominee to constituents as they went through the line, often in Spanish.

"There's many people, many voters as well as electeds in this part of the district, that had a longstanding relationship with Congressmember Espaillat," Rivera told CNN in an interview at the event. "That ship has sailed. She actually won the seat. Now it's her job to actually do this type of work."

Sometimes that has forced her to confront voters whose views are far from her own. During her interview with CNN, Avila Chevalier was flagged down by a group of voters sitting in Marcus Garvey Park. The Democratic nominee struck up a conversation with Monique Wyche, a restaurant employee and small business owner who grew up in Harlem.

When Wyche brought up the Iran War, Avila Chevalier argued that the money spent on it could have gone towards universal childcare. When the topic turned to immigration, Wyche said that while ICE's actions were "sick," she was concerned about migrants not paying taxes, a claim Avila Chevalier quickly refuted.

"Actually, they do get taxed," Avila Chevalier said. "I think that narrative actually benefits corporations, and so they don't pay taxes."

The two went back and forth for nearly 10 minutes, with Wyche calling on Avila Chevalier to work with both Republicans and Democrats while also charting her own path in Congress.

That is what Avila Chevalier says she signed up for — having hard conversations with people to make sense of the world and bridge the gap between what exists and what could be – and what she hopes to bring to Congress next year.

"Organizing is about meeting people where they're at," she said. "It is deeply unsexy work."

articles.title: ‘Radical’ has become the political word of the summer
articles.summary: As campaigns prepare for the crucial fall stretch ahead of the midterm elections, the word “radical” is being slung against candidates on both sides of the aisle. It’s happening as both parties are pulled from the political center, and it’s being used by Republicans against Democrats and Democrats against Republicans to make the same argument:…
articles.body:
As campaigns prepare for the crucial fall stretch ahead of the midterm elections, the word “radical” is being slung against candidates on both sides of the aisle.

It’s happening as both parties are pulled from the political center, and it’s being used by Republicans against Democrats and Democrats against Republicans to make the same argument: My opponent has moved outside the mainstream.

Republicans, often on their heels because of negative headwinds from the economy and the war in Iran, have used the term regularly as a weapon against “radical” Democrats.

From President Trump down to congressional campaigns, the GOP is eager to shift attention to how the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the left rank of the Democratic Party in general is “radical” or “extreme.”

Democrats, for their part, have used “radical” as a way to describe Trump and his MAGA movement, arguing it is time to put a curb on the GOP.

“Radical is the current word of choice in the framing battle to set the agenda for the 2026 elections,” said Tobe Berkovitz, a communications professor emeritus at Boston University who has served as a political consultant. “The Democrats and Republicans both use it to position their opponents as far out of touch with current social and political norms.

“For framing to succeed, words must be used repeatedly to sink into the minds of the voter,” Berkovitz added. “‘Radical’ certainly fits that criteria.”

For both Republicans and Democrats, “the partisan struggle to define ‘radical will be a very important part of the campaign cycle,” said Julian Zelizer, a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University.

The race to define the meaning of the word has been at the forefront of political battles around the country.

In Florida, GOP Rep. Byron Donalds, who is campaigning for governor, has been using the word in a political ad against his opponent, Democrat David Jolly, who used to be a Republican House member.

“How radical is David Jolly on the trans agenda?” the 30-second spot begins.

It continues by saying that Jolly is “radically liberal, radically wrong.”

“The only way you defeat crazy is stand up to it,” Donalds says in the conclusion of the ad.

The use of radical extended to the back-and-forth between the White House and Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), who is up for reelection in November, after Ossoff slammed Trump for not prioritizing his job as president.

“He golfs and trades stocks. … He wants to build a ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar,” Ossoff said at a rally last weekend, referencing White House aide Natalie Harp and beginning a days-long feud with the White House.

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung responded by slamming Ossoff for being “a radical, extremist” Democrat.

Trump has time and again referred to Democrats as “radical” or “the radical left,” but he refrained from using the rhetoric when he was asked about Ossoff by a reporter in the Oval Office. The president simply called him “Pee-wee Herman” after the comic personality played by the late actor Paul Reubens.

Democrats — from individual campaigns to EMILY’s List, the Democratic PAC that helps elect women — have also made radical part of their regular vernacular.

Earlier this month, for example, the Democratic Governors Association released an ad highlighting Rep. Tom Tiffany’s (R-Wis.) “radical agenda.” Tiffany is facing off against David Crowley in the closely watched Wisconsin gubernatorial race.

“Pandering politician Tom Tiffany pretends he’s anything but a congressman with a MAGA agenda,” a narrator says. “The truth? Tiffany’s agenda is so radical that even Republicans say he’s part of a group of legislative terrorists in Congress.”

In Illinois, Gov. JB Pritzker, up for reelection, has been knocking his opponent Darren Bailey for being too radical. In a new ad called “Too Extreme,” Pritzker targets his opponent’s views opposing abortion, including in cases of rape and incest, as well as his loyalty to Trump and his “radical” pro-gun rhetoric.

Political observers say the word perfectly describes the polarization of the moment.

“It means more now than it ever did before,” said Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist. “It’s actually more reflective of where both parties are now.”

“It’s an exclamation point on the ideas, and it’s shorthand for out of the norm,” Del Percio added.

But Del Percio, who does not support Trump, said using the word in a broad-sweeping way is “ineffective.”

“It’s laughable in some cases because someone like David Jolly is anything but radical,” she said. “He’s a former Republican and is much more independent minded. You can’t take the DSA movement and their ideas and impose that on David Jolly.”

She suggested it’s much more effective for Republican Mike Rogers to use the label on someone like Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race. “His policies are associated with radical ideas,” she said.

But Republican strategist Brian Seitchik said the word resonates with voters because “it transforms Democratic policy disagreements into a warning about the people proposing it.”

“It makes Democrats not just wrong but willing to remake the world with their policies that are not mainstream, that do not resonate with the American people,” Seitchik said. “We are not a socialist country. We are not Europe, despite the socialist agenda that is taking over the Democratic Party.”

Still, Seitchik cautioned, “You can’t just point and say ‘radical.’ You have to have some meat on the bones. And thankfully Democrats are giving us plenty of opportunities to do that.”

Michael Eric Dyson, the renowned historian and author, called the rhetoric the Red Scare 2.0, particularly for Republicans — and even for some moderate Democrats — who have seen the rise of candidates like Zohran Mamdani in New York, El-Sayed in Michigan, and Angie Nixon in Florida.

As the races heat up, he and others predicted, the rhetoric will only ramp up.

“It’s definitely a scare tactic,” Dyson said. “When you ain’t got much to say you got to do that. You got to play the card you got. And it’s a joker.”

articles.title: Iowa Senate candidates zero in on cancer crisis as key race tightens
articles.summary: Candidates for Iowa’s open Senate seat are zeroing in on the state’s high rate of cancer diagnoses as the race emerges as one of the most unexpectedly competitive contests this cycle. The race features Democratic state legislator Josh Turek challenging Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson (Iowa) for the seat held by retiring Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst…
articles.body:
Candidates for Iowa’s open Senate seat are zeroing in on the state’s high rate of cancer diagnoses as the race emerges as one of the most unexpectedly competitive contests this cycle.

The race features Democratic state legislator Josh Turek challenging Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson (Iowa) for the seat held by retiring Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst (R). The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election analyst, last week moved the state’s Senate contest from “lean Republican” to “toss-up.”

Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist in basketball, is emphasizing his bipartisan record, trying to pitch himself as an independent voice. His latest ad notes that he has voted with Republicans in the statehouse 700 times. Hinson, a former broadcast journalist, is leaning on her record leading bipartisan bills and overseeing appropriations in the House. She also carries an endorsement from President Trump.

But an X factor is each candidate’s approach to Iowa’s cancer rates, which are some of the worst in the country. Iowa has the second-highest incidence rate for cancer in the nation, behind only Kentucky, and that rate is rising while most of the country’s incidence rates are stable or decreasing.

Kerri Johannsen, the senior director of policy and programs at the Iowa Environmental Council (IEC), said knowing many people with cancer was common around the state when she and her team started researching the crisis last summer.

“We all knew a lot of people, of course, who had cancer,” Johannsen said. “But I think that there was an idea that it was kind of just normal.”

The biggest culprits, according to IEC’s research, are environmental contaminants, especially PFAS, nitrates, radon and pesticides — the levels of which are higher in Iowa than other states.

“You can’t ever say like, ‘This thing caused this cancer,’ but we do have what we call kind of a skyscraper of risk factors,” Johannsen said. “And when you start to say, okay, well, maybe you have radon in your home. That’s a carcinogen. On top of that, perhaps you’ve had exposure to pesticides or nitrate in your drinking water. Each of those things, when they stack on top of each other, increases the risk of developing cancer.”

The prominence of pesticides and nitrates, in particular, are due to the heavily agricultural economy that makes Iowa run.

Johannsen said those spreading awareness of the issue have to carefully thread a needle between discussing solutions and not demonizing the agriculture industry that is the backbone of the state.

“I’m a farmer’s daughter,” Johannsen said, noting that while she understands “this is a tough thing to talk about,” the IEC has found that “the elephant in the room when it comes to this issue is: What part is our industrialized agricultural system playing in this crisis?”

“Many people in Iowa already were feeling and suspecting this was a part of the problem,” she continued.

The candidates for political offices are taking that balance seriously.

Turek has been talking a lot about cancer as he travels the state. He has told stories about his grandmother, who died of pancreatic cancer; his father, who was exposed to Agent Orange and had a variety of health complications including cancer; and his sister, who was diagnosed with Stage 2 breast cancer the day Turek launched his campaign for Senate.

His message is focused on cracking down on insurance companies so patients have more access to care they can afford.

“I talk a lot about healthcare as a human right, and that if I’m able to get to the U.S. Senate, I want to fight for a public option to make sure that every single American has access to a baseline level of healthcare coverage,” he said in an interview with Ability Magazine published earlier this month.

Hinson, in a statement to The Hill, said she supports efforts to address the growing cancer rate by expanding access to detection and care.

“I’m proud to co-lead legislation that would improve access to mammogram machines, mobile cancer screening tools, and other preventative equipment in rural areas,” Hinson said. “We’ve got way more to do – I’ll keep fighting for results that help families fight cancer and save lives.”

Hinson also introduced a bill recently that would redirect revenue from existing taxes on tobacco into cancer research, and a spokesperson pointed to her involvement in passing the Rural Health Transformation Fund as part of last year’s Republican reconciliation package, the One Big Beautiful Bill.

The focus on cancer rates comes as the race for Senate tightens.

A red stronghold for the past decade, the agricultural prairie state has taken a heavy hit from Trump’s tariffs and rising fertilizer prices. At the same time, Republican candidates nationwide are bogged down by the Trump administration’s low approval ratings.

In announcing the seat’s shift to “toss-up,” the Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor wrote that “the political environment is uniquely challenging for the GOP” in Iowa.

An Emerson College poll earlier this month found Hinson leading Turek, 48 percent to 45 percent, within the poll’s credibility interval. Six percent of respondents were undecided.

The Cook report also shifted the governor’s race from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat.” And the gubernatorial candidates, Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn, have made a central issue of addressing the cancer crisis.

Sand this week took it a step further, using headlines about a new mRNA treatment for melanoma to bash Lahn over his skepticism of mRNA vaccines.

Lahn, speaking at an American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network roundtable on Tuesday, singled out water quality as a cause for colon and ovarian cancer rates rising and said addressing contaminants in Iowa’s food and water supply is a “major, major focus.” He has also talked about his father’s battle with non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Timothy Hagle, a professor of political science at the University of Iowa, said he’d seen the cancer crisis showing up in races all across the ballot, including the three competitive House races. In particular, Democrats are hitting Republicans over their votes to cut cancer research and funding for care in the reconciliation bill last year.

“I did see at least a couple of ads, not from Turek directly, but from some of the PACs that are advertising against Hinson, that kind of were chastising her for votes that she took in Congress, and so it’s sort of an indirect way to get at some of these medical issues,” Hagle said.

Turek has said as much on the campaign trail.

“Looking at a state with a legitimate healthcare crisis,” Turek said in June. “Only state with a growing cancer rate. Closed 250 more healthcare clinics than we’ve opened and what has she [Hinson] done? She has voted to see 110,000 Iowans lose their healthcare.”

But Hagle predicted the race will mostly turn on more conventional issues, like name recognition. Turek is still trying to introduce himself to voters, Hagle said, while Hinson as a U.S. representative is better-known. It’s the reverse in the governor’s race, though, where Sand as state auditor cut an outsized profile and is making pains to distinguish himself from other Democrats.

“The hope is that to the extent that Sand might actually win, that he’ll cause the other Democrats and the other competitive races to do better, which is probably one of the reasons why some people think that the Senate race is a toss-up at this point,” Hagle said. “But I’m just not buying it, at least not yet.”

articles.title: Four states where Democrats are running away from their own brand
articles.summary: A party confident in its own name doesn’t need to find ways not to use it.
articles.body:
When Democrat David Roth suspended his U.S. Senate campaign in Idaho on July 28, he did not mention the man his exit was intended to benefit. Todd Achilles, a former Democratic state representative, is now running as an independent against Sen. Jim Risch (R-Idaho). When he called it a two-person race, he didn’t mention Roth either.

Neither man wanted to draw attention to what had just happened.

That silence was notable, because this wasn’t an isolated incident. It’s the third time this cycle a Democratic Senate nominee has stepped aside to let a supposedly independent candidate — or at least someone without an official “D” next to his name — take the field alone against a Republican incumbent.

Individually, each case looks like a local story about a longshot candidate fizzling out. Together, though they look like a nationwide Democratic strategy — something the party would certainly never admit to, and one that says more about the state of the Democratic brand than its leaders likely want to discuss.

In Nebraska, Cindy Burbank won the Democratic Senate primary in May after openly promising she would drop out if she saw no path to victory. She kept that promise on July 17, exiting the race just as independent Dan Osborn qualified for the ballot by petition. This set up a one-on-one race against Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.). The secretary of state had already tried to remove Burbank from the ballot for not being a “good-faith candidate.” She sued her way back on, then dropped out to help Osborn, exactly as expected.

In South Dakota, Democrat Julian Beaudion dropped out in early August after months of insisting he’d never quit the race. A former state trooper, Beaudion looked like an ideal Democratic candidate on paper. But the challenge to Sen. Mike Rounds (R-N.D.) will now fall to independent Brian Bengs, a former Democrat who was trounced by Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.) in 2022.

In Idaho, the Ada County Democratic Central Committee — covering Boise, the state’s Democratic stronghold — sent Roth a public ultimatum in early July: Raise real money and produce a new plan, or the party would consider endorsing Achilles instead. Roth had raised just over $8,000 to Achilles’ $700,000 and Risch’s $3.5 million. Roth called the demand “ridiculous” and vowed to stay in, but three weeks later, he dropped out without explanation.

The same conversation is happening in Montana. Democratic nominee Alani Bankhead (D) has so far refused pressure to withdraw in favor of independent Seth Bodnar, even after the state party chair was found to have quietly solicited legal advice on handling a potential vacancy.

Four states, four Republican-held Senate seats, four Democratic parties pulling or considering the same maneuver of vacating their own ballot line so that a technically unaffiliated candidate can run without the baggage of the Democratic label.

None of this is illegal, and it’s not new — Angus King and Bernie Sanders have caucused with Senate Democrats for years without anyone calling it a scandal. What’s new is the intentionality. National Democrats aren’t just tolerating friendly independents anymore; in at least two of these races, state party infrastructure actively worked to clear the field for them.

It makes a certain amount of sense. In states like these, “Democrat” is usually a losing brand in statewide races, regardless of a candidate’s actual positions. An independent can absorb anti-incumbent energy and deep-red dissatisfaction with national Republicans in ways a Democratic nominee simply cannot, no matter how moderate that nominee might be.

Timing matters, too. These withdrawals are landing just as centrist Democrats panic over the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America. The New York Times recently reported that Third Way and other centrist organizations are preparing for what one leader called the “next war” — not against Republicans, but against the party’s own socialist wing, newly emboldened by Senate primary victories by Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed (D) and Florida’s Angie Nixon (D).

Democrats are purging their brand from red-state ballots and bracing for a civil war over that same brand everywhere else. When a party isn’t sure what it stands for, it is easier just not to say anything.

Idaho Democrats had made a habit of swapping candidates on their own ballot line, but the legislature closed that loophole in 2025, declaring that the winner of the primary must be the candidate in November, barring death or disqualification. Simply withdrawing in favor of an independent does not violate that law, but it is still a betrayal of the party’s own voters.

How voters respond to this nationwide strategy remains to be seen. The independents in these four races still trail their Republican opponents in the polls and in fundraising. But the strategy tells on itself. A party confident in its own name doesn’t need to find ways not to use it. Is that shrewd coalition building? Or a quiet admission of brand failure? It depends on which Democrat you ask.

Brian Almon is chairman of Idaho’s District 14 Republican Party, a trustee of the Eagle Public Library Board, and editor of the Gem State Chronicle.
