articles.title: Canadian anger reaches fever pitch over Trump’s tariff war
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Canada pledges tit-for-tat tariffs ▪ Jeffries, Kushner meet ahead of midterms ▪ Economic ‘D-Day’ for Iran ▪ House Ethics Committee under pressure Canada’s political leaders have united to rally the country against President Trump in a brewing trade war after Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from talks on Friday just hours before new…
articles.body:
▪ Jeffries, Kushner meet ahead of midterms

Canada’s political leaders have united to rally the country against President Trump in a brewing trade war after Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from talks on Friday just hours before new 50 percent tariffs took effect.

Carney told reporters at a press conference in Ottawa that his government will “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar.” Retaliatory tariffs are set to take effect on Sept. 8.

Carney said he broke off negotiations reluctantly because he knows the tariffs will result in higher costs for Canadians.

“But at the same time, we take this step confident that it is in the best interest of Canada,” he said.

“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” Carney added. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked.”

Canadian politicians across the political spectrum have backed Carney’s move, including opposition leader Pierre Poilievre of the Conservative Party.

“Canadians must stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses,” he wrote on the social platform X after talks broke down. “Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal. Instead, we must continue the fight for tariff-free trade.”

Provincial premiers struck a similar note.

“I’m sure there is a desire to get back to the table, but we should recognize that the Trump administration and the president are deeply flawed. He’s got two more years left in office. We should be prepared to duke it out for two years. And then hopefully sanity will return to America,” Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew told reporters .

“It will be painful, but we have a strong, vibrant, diversified economy,” said Ontario Premier Doug Ford , who has led Canada’s opposition to Trump’s trade policies.

“We have to use every tool in our toolbox to make sure as Donald Trump is trying to inflict pain on every Canadian that we inflict pain right back,” he added in remarks to reporters.

Conservative Alberta Premier Danielle Smith expressed concern about the impact of a trade war but said the U.S.’s terms in negotiations were “untenable” for Canada to accept.

Trump is not enjoying similar unity behind his trade policies, which have been among the most controversial aspects of his second term.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), a moderate who is in the midst of a tough reelection battle, urged the administration to “consider the negative impact” of engaging in a trade war with Canada. She said the tariffs would result in higher costs for Mainers.

“Ever since the tariffs were first announced, I have heard from many businesses, farmers, and lobstermen concerned about the cost of navigating the tariffs, the lack of domestic supply chains, and the likely imposition of retaliatory tariffs by Canada,” she said in a post on X . “I urge both sides to return to the negotiating table.”

Democrats were predictably furious over the development, with figures including Sen. Amy Klobuchar , who is running for governor of Minnesota, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul warning that prices would go up for U.S. consumers.

The U.S. and Canada had seemed to be approaching a deal that would stave off the 50 percent tariffs from going into effect on more than $20 billion worth of Canadian goods through much of last week.

The tariffs affect a wide range of goods, including wine, cement, plywood, furniture and hockey sticks.

Carney said “significant progress” was made in recent weeks but accused the U.S. of seeking to change the terms at the last minute.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued in an interview with The New York Times that the U.S. proposal would have given Canada the most preferential treatment of any trading partner.

He said the Trump administration would have eliminated a 10 percent tariff on softwood lumber and reduce a 25 percent tariff on cars that were imposed last year. He said the U.S. also offered to lower tariffs on metals, including steel and aluminum.

Carney said at the press conference that Canada agreed to many U.S. demands, including lifting various retaliatory tariffs and convincing Canadian provinces to lift bans on the sale of U.S. liquor. But he said the U.S. refused to include exemptions for some Canadian trucks and subsidies for French culture.

Trump showed no signs of backing down Sunday, alleging Canada wants the “benefits of being a state, without being one.”

“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” he said on Truth Social.

▪ The Hill : Sean Duffy says Carney will ‘come to the table.’

▪ Politico : Inside the 72 hours that cratered the U.S.-Canada deal.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta has called off settlement talks with Paramount over the state’s lawsuit against its planned acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Bonta, one of 12 state attorneys general suing the company, accused Paramount of leaking details of a meeting they held Friday and misrepresenting the talks.

U.S. Southern Command carried out an airstrike on an alleged drug trafficking boat in the East Pacific, the first known such strike in two months. Southcom said two people were killed in the attack. More than 200 people have been killed over the past year and a half of U.S. strikes in the Pacific and the Caribbean.

Sean Grayson, the former sheriff’s deputy convicted of fatally shooting Sonya Massey at her home in Illinois in 2024, has died in prison at age 32 after just six months into his 20-year sentence. He was previously denied early release as he was suffering from advanced colon cancer.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill, on July 13, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana )

MEETING OF THE MINDS : House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) and the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met in private in recent weeks to discuss possible areas of common ground, five people with knowledge of the meeting told The New York Times .

The meeting is being interpreted as a sign of the administration’s acknowledgement of the likelihood that Democrats win back control of the House in November.

The Decision Desk HQ forecast model currently gives Democrats roughly a 2 in 3 chance of winning a majority this fall.

Two people told the Times that Jeffries and Kushner discussed housing, immigration and the cost of living as potential areas of progress, and Kushner suggested Jeffries could meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles .

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) downplayed the significance of the meeting during an appearance on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing,” noting that Kushner doesn’t have an official position within the administration. Kushner has served as an informal envoy for the president in talks to end the conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran.

Trump and Jeffries have often clashed since the president’s return to officer. However, Trump told Punchbowl News earlier this month that he believes Jeffries is a “nice guy” with whom he could do business.

The Times reported that Kushner has told Trump’s advisers that if any bipartisan accomplishments are to get done in Congress, Jeffries, a fellow New Yorker, is the most serious person among Democratic leaders.

▪ The Hill : ‘Shocking’ fake poll firm puts industry under the microscope.

▪ The Hill : ‘Radical’ has become the political word of the summer.

‘D-DAY’ ARRIVING : Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) said Monday will be economic “D-Day” for Iran as Trump has vowed to inflict maximum economic pressure on the country to force it to agree to end the war.

“Their economy is in shambles. And they’re still dangerous. So, the president’s right to focus on it. And now he’s going even further economically. And as you said, tomorrow is D-Day for the economy in Iran,” Barrasso said on Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures.”

The Trump administration’s main tool for the economic offensive is the use of secondary sanctions, in which the U.S. will penalize foreign nations, banks and businesses that work with Iran economically.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is scheduled to reveal the full details of the plan at a press conference today.

“We are now entering the endgame,” Bessent wrote on X, teasing an article he wrote for The Financial Times . “At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary.”

Iran has warned its neighbors in the region against joining the U.S. in an “economic war” against Tehran, saying it will “retaliate in a seismic manner” if Trump takes action.

▪ The Hill Insider : Trump’s ‘economic D-Day’ on Iran puts China in the crosshairs.

▪ The Hill : Mike Pence says more U.S. strikes against Iran ‘inevitable.’

▪ PBS : Iran’s president says U.S. memorandum is best way out of war.

RUNWAY CLEAR : The Trump administration has begun deportation flights of migrants previously protected under temporary protected status (TPS) after the last roadblock was lifted.

A federal judge lifted the final stay that barred immigration authorities from carrying out deportations to Ethiopia last week, the last of various court cases from TPS recipients challenging the elimination of their protections.

There are 13 countries formerly part of TPS that past administrations deemed not stable enough because of civil unrest or natural disasters to safely return migrants. Rebecca Beitsch reports for The Hill’s Insider that the designations for four other countries still part of TPS are set to expire soon, meaning more than 1.3 million migrants either have or will likely soon lose their protected status.

“Effectively, this signals the end of the program,” Nayna Gupta , policy director at the American Immigration Council, told Beitsch.

The moves come after the Supreme Court’s ruling in June that courts didn’t have the power to review the administration’s decision to end protections for citizens of Haiti and Syria.

▪ The Hill : Florida Republican ‘working’ with Haiti to stabilize government.

▪ The Hill : Federal judge rules against Trump’s 75-country visa ban.

The president will participate in a Rose Garden event at 2:30 p.m. He will participate in two telerallies at 6 p.m. and 7 p.m.

The House will convene at 9 a.m. for a pro forma session.

The Senate will meet at 12:30 p.m. for a pro forma session.

Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) arrives for new member orientation check-in and program registration in Washington, Nov. 13, 2022.

HURRY UP : Democrats and Republicans are calling on the House Ethics Committee to move more expeditiously in its investigations into members accused of sexual misconduct or domestic violence.

The probes into Reps. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), Max Miller (R-Ohio) and Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.) have dominated headlines for weeks and left the public in limbo as the latter two are seeking reelection in November. Mills was defeated in his primary last week.

“One of the long-standing problems of House Ethics investigations is that they simply take too long — staff, the public, and the Members need the investigations and reporting to be quicker and responsive,” Rep. Teresa Leger Fern ández (D-N.M.), the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, told The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi .

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) argued on X earlier this month that the current Ethics process has a “massive problem,” saying “slow rolling investigations to protect party members is not due process. It is a cover up.”

The Democratic Women’s Caucus urged the panel to give an update on the status of their investigation into Gomez before the 60-day “blackout period” ahead of Election Day, which starts at the end of next week.

House Ethics Committee Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) told Bloomberg in April that the panel would be “receptive” to changes to speed up investigations.

▪ The Washington Post : The police investigation into how Miller’s daughter got hurt.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky looks on during his meeting with President Trump on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, on July 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

NOT NOW : Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky rejected a call from his former defense chief for the country to hold new elections, saying that doing so during wartime would “split Ukraine apart.”

Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for an election last week in the aftermath of his firing from his role overseeing the country’s armed forces. Fedorov was popular and credited with helping modernize Ukraine’s forces with new technology and drone warfare, but Zelensky ousted him as Fedorov clashed with Ukraine’s top military commander.

Zelensky told reporters that holding elections now, still in the midst of war with Russia, would “pose enormous risks.”

“I believe elections during a war like this would generally pose enormous risks. Holding elections right now would be a tsunami for the state that would split Ukraine apart,” he said, according to The Associated Press .

Zelensky noted it was not the first such call but said no one has come up with a plan for holding elections safely, legitimately and democratically. Holding elections now would be complicated by the Ukrainian territory and citizens currently under Russian occupation, the Ukrainians who have fled abroad and those currently fighting on the front lines.

Trump and his allies have also previously called for Ukrainian elections, with the president even calling Zelensky a dictator. Ukraine noted the remarks seemed to echo a Russian disinformation campaign.

A presidential election was set to be held in 2024 but was postponed indefinitely amid the war. Zelensky said last year that he wouldn’t seek reelection to a second term after the war ends.

▪ CNN : Russia likely to mobilize 300,000 more troops, Zelensky says.

▪ The Guardian : Russia withdraws ambassador to U.K.

The right to worship shall not be infringed , Anti-Defamation League CEO and National Director Jonathan Greenblatt writes in The Hill.

Virginia may be building a national model for corrections , Jeff Bennett writes in The Hill.

Kyle Kirkwood poses for a photo after winning the IndyCar Freedom 250 Grand Prix auto race in Washington, on Aug. 23, 2026.

And finally … IndyCar driver Kyle Kirkwood won the Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington, D.C., on Sunday, capping off the summer of semiquincentennial events.

Kirkwood led the pack for most of the 147 laps, equal to 250 miles total, throughout the streets of the nation’s capital, passing by several key landmarks of the city. The cars reached speeds as high as 180 miles per hour during the race.

First lady Melania Trump took part in a relatively rare interview during the race, sharing how her father got her into racing as she was growing up.

“So, he introduced me to [the] design of the cars and the mechanics, and also the speed, and I loved it, every minute of it,” she said.

The president first called for the race in January, authorizing it with an executive order.

articles.title: Congress must now do its part on Medicare fraud
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance urged Congress to codify recent healthcare fraud enforcement successes into permanent law to prevent future administrations from undoing the current administration’s progress.
articles.body:
When Vice President JD Vance — President Trump’s appointed fraud czar — stood before the Cabinet at Camp David at the end of July, he rattled off some eye-popping numbers. His team had uncovered $230 billion in fraud and stopped $56 billion of it before a dime went out the door.

A week later, Vance took the same case to Capitol Hill, hosting a roundtable with lawmakers and urging Congress to make the crackdown permanent rather than let it lapse with a future change in executive leadership.

Congress should heed his advice, and quickly. The relevant committees — Senate Finance and House Energy and Commerce chief among them — should draft legislation this fall that locks in the Medicare and Medicaid’s enforcement authority, funding levels, and enrollment moratoriums by statute.

Otherwise, everything this administration has built through executive and regulatory action can be undone the same way: by a future administration that simply chooses not to enforce the law. Only Congress can make these wins permanent.

The case for urgency is not abstract. Just this month, prosecutors in Philadelphia unsealed charges against 19 people in a home-healthcare scheme that reads almost like parody. One caregiver allegedly billed for visits made while she was traveling abroad. Another claimed to be caring for seven patients at once, racking up more billed hours than exist in a single day. The government says that one fraud ring alone cost taxpayers more than $4 million.

That is the kind of abuse the administration’s crackdown is built to catch. Under Health and Human Services Director Robert F. Kennedy Jr., CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and Center for Medicare Director John Brooks, the executive branch has suspended billions of dollars in suspect Medicare payments, imposed nationwide moratoriums on new enrollment for hospice, home health , and durable medical equipment suppliers, and revoked billing privileges from thousands of providers.

This year’s national health care fraud takedown produced charges against more than 450 defendants tied to roughly $6 billion in alleged false claims. California and Minnesota have had more than $1 billion in Medicaid reimbursements frozen while they prove the money is reaching real patients.

But the same enforcement tools that catch fraud can just as easily overcorrect and choke off legitimate care — which is exactly why these decisions should not be left to agency discretion alone.

Take remote patient monitoring, the technology that lets seniors managing diabetes, high blood pressure, or heart disease take readings at home and send them straight to their care team, instead of waiting months for an appointment or driving hundreds of miles to a doctor’s office.

Regulators recently found real fraud in the program: companies cold-calling or robocalling seniors into monitoring plans they never asked for, then billing Medicare for monitoring that did not meaningfully happen. CMS deserves credit for catching it. But unelected career staff have now drafted a proposal broad enough to effectively kill physicians’ ability to use outside companies to run remote patient monitoring at all — even though those companies are often what keeps monitoring running for practices too short-staffed to do it themselves, in a country already facing a serious doctor shortage .

The problem with leaving fixes to rulemaking is that it makes overbroad fixes more likely. And either way, a future administrator can rewrite it again.

Congress doesn’t have that problem. Lawmakers could write a fix directly into statute — banning the cold-calling of beneficiaries that has fueled most of the abuse, and requiring a physician’s sign-off before any patient is enrolled. As the Heritage Foundation’s Peter St. Onge has noted , those two changes alone would stop most of the fraud without gutting a program that seniors, especially in underserved rural areas, depend on.

And that’s exactly what Congress should be across the board. It should take the enforcement gains the administration has already made, and the fixes still being worked out at the agency level, and write them into law before the moment passes.

Protecting Medicare from fraud should not be a partisan project. Both parties have an interest in a program that serves the seniors who paid into it for decades. The administration has done its part; the crackdown has been thorough and, so far, effective. As Vance made clear on Capitol Hill, the next move belongs to Congress. Lawmakers should introduce that bill while they still have the momentum to get it done.

Thomas Stratmann is a senior research fellow at the Mercatus Center and a professor of economics and law at George Mason University. He has a health economics research focus.

(AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

articles.title: Is it finally time for a female president?
articles.summary: The next presidential election is more than two years away, but several women are already mentioned as possible candidates.
articles.body:
More than 200 women have sought the U.S. presidency in the last 250 years. Only Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Kamala Harris in 2024 became major-party nominees. No woman has ever won the nation’s most consequential job.

The next presidential election is more than two years away, but several women are already mentioned as possible candidates. Voters will be asked again to decide whether America is ready to elect its first female president. But that is the wrong question.

The correct question, of course, is which candidate has the right skills and qualities to lead America at this point in history. Voters shouldn’t select or reject a presidential candidate just because she’s a woman. Gender should not be a factor. The time will come when a woman finally breaks through the shatter-resistant ceiling that female candidates have encountered for so long. That ceiling is beginning to show some cracks, but it’s still fortified by stereotypes.

Politico reports that “Americans remain wary of electing a female president.” An American University poll “reveals a complicated portrait of how voters view women in politics.” Voters want to see more women in public office, but “bias and narrow expectations” surface when voters react to women in our highest office.

What expectations? “Empathy, inclusivity, and fresh perspectives are widely seen as unique strengths women bring to elected roles,” the poll found . However, while women are most trusted to address family-related issues, men are more trusted to deal with national security, foreign adversaries, crime and global conflicts.

“Women candidates also face a ‘double bind,'” states the poll’s write-up — they need to be “both ‘tough’ and ‘likable,’ a standard not typically applied to their male counterparts.”

Yet, tough and likable are not mutually exclusive qualities; empathy is not unique to women; and men care about family issues, too. Until voters shed these biases, they will deprive the country of some of its most talented and promising leaders.

At the same time, America would benefit from some of the qualities typically associated with women. The country is suffering from a hot mess of hypermasculinity. The president bullies and abuses allies. Pete Hegseth can’t get enough testosterone. Kash Patel acts like a frat bro. Stephen Miller has deported empathy from immigration policy. Whoever inherits the White House will have to dedicate enormous time, energy and political capital to repairing what’s left of government and reviving the rest of the world’s trust in America. That will require considerable “empathy, inclusivity, and fresh perspectives.”

Those are not inherently female qualities; they are human qualities traditionally coded as feminine. Voters need to make a significant attitude adjustment. They must understand the extraordinary value of the softer attributes, particularly as we try to heal the country and its relationships abroad. And they must broaden their understanding of toughness.

The 48th president will have to be a healer, a unifier, a firm but principled leader, sympathetic to the American people’s needs, reluctant to make war, and open to cooperation with the rest of the world. He or she must acknowledge that bullying and isolationism don’t work in a thoroughly interconnected world.

At this moment, we need a strong leader, but also a more mature understanding of what strength entails. It’s genuine rather than performative. It’s found in friendships, not isolation. It acknowledges, corrects and learns from mistakes, rather than distracting us from them. It serves the people rather than the person. At the same time, he or she must stand up to tyrants rather than becoming one of them. And while it remains true that America must defend peace with strength, strength means much more than military muscle. It requires domestic unity, the commitment to a common vision, and a commitment to one another.

I mentioned some early cracks in the shatter-proof ceiling. A study published in Political Behavior indicates that the process of redefining presidential strength may already be underway. “The traits that people associate with women politicians are more positive than 10 years ago and more congruent to desirable traits for politicians,” the researchers found.

Concurrently, respect for stereotypical male politicians and politics “shows a strong downfall compared to a decade ago.” The more positive view of women politicians and more negative view of their male counterparts corresponds with the Trump era.

Will there be a candidate who combines the best qualities of both? That’s what we should watch for as the next group of candidates emerges for the 2028 election.

William S. Becker is co-editor of and a contributor to “ Democracy Unchained: How to Rebuild Government for the People,” and a contributor to Democracy in a Hotter Time , named by the journal Nature as one of 2023’s five best science books. He previously served as a senior official in the Wisconsin Department of Justice. He is currently executive director of the Presidential Climate Action Project.

articles.title: Kyle Kirkwood wins Freedom 250 Grand Prix as IndyCar takes over DC
articles.summary: Kyle Kirkwood, an American IndyCar driver racing for Andretti Global, took home the checkered flag Sunday with a win at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, the first professional motorsports road race ever run on the streets of Washington, D.C. The event, which was billed as a de facto finale to a slew of “America 250”…
articles.body:
Kyle Kirkwood, an American IndyCar driver racing for Andretti Global, took home the checkered flag Sunday with a win at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix , the first professional motorsports road race ever run on the streets of Washington, D.C.

The event, which was billed as a de facto finale to a slew of “America 250” celebrations in the District this summer, was heavy on symbols of American pride and attended by President Trump and other top Cabinet officials.

Sunday’s race day drew tens of thousands to the nation’s capital and shuttered much of the National Mall and downtown D.C. in the days leading up to the event.

With his win, Kirkwood notched his seventh career IndyCar victory and his sixth on a street course, raking in key IndyCar series points with just two weeks remaining in the racing league’s season.

A Jupiter, Fla., native and one of eight Americans in the field, Kirkwood made a point of referencing Trump directly during a postrace interview after speeding away with a lead that lasted more than 125 laps on Sunday.

“I’m almost in tears here. This is a big moment for us and a big moment for America with the 250,” Kirkwood said.

“I’m a fellow Florida guy, I live up in Jupiter,” he said, pointing to the area where the president was watching. “It’s cool to see him down here. And what a place to do it. If you can’t win the Indy 500, this is definitely the place to win.”

Trump began Sunday’s race by waving the green flag after his motorcade drove a ceremonial first lap around the 1.7-mile track featuring seven turns and weaving through some of D.C.’s most iconic monuments and federal buildings.

Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum was seen on television coverage atop the pre-race podium and screamed into a microphone when it was time for drivers to “start your engines.”

Burgum is one of several top Trump officials who had been tasked with selling the event as a moment of unity for the country, even as local critics raised noise and vibration concerns.

“This is the perfect time to do this. Congress is on recess, the economic development of D.C., the people here all love this idea,” Burgum argued during an interview on Fox News just hours before the race.

“I’m a DC resident. Please DON’T do this again next year,” wrote the left-leaning influencer and media personality Aaron Parnas on the social platform X, responding to a clip of Burgum’s remark.

The president was seen visiting with top government leaders, business officials and executives at IndyCar during the nearly three-hour-long race, while Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was tasked with waving the checkered flag as Kirkwood soared through the finish line.

Kirkwood finished four seconds ahead of Denmark native Christian Lundgaard, averaging 93.2 mph and gaining an additional 40 IndyCar Series points on leader Álex Palou, one of the icons of the sport who struggled in D.C. on Sunday, finishing 20th out of 25.

Throughout the weekend, the roars of the IndyCar and bustling pit crews could be heard for blocks across downtown, as some residents complained about traffic, long lines to get into the racetrack and noisy flyovers as part of the celebration.

Elected Democrats, meanwhile, suggested Sunday’s first-of-its-kind event sent an out-of-touch message to Americans across the country.

“While you struggle with the cost of gas, Trump offers you the spectacle of an IndyCar race hoping you will not notice,” Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) wrote in one social media post on Sunday. “More taxpayer money spent on his self-aggrandizing distractions. And you get higher taxes and higher costs.”

College football begins this weekend, thrusting a debate about the future of what it means to be a student-athlete into the spotlight once again. Some observers expressed outrage online over reports that star University of South Carolina quarterback LaNorris Sellers is not taking any classes this fall before he graduates this December. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who has yet to signal support for the Protect College Sports Act, responded in a social media post that he had proposed an amendment requiring athletes to be enrolled and making progress toward a degree. “We are seeing too many cases where the ‘student’ in student-athlete is becoming optional,” the Republican said.

Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) appears to be enjoying his recess. The Republican spent the weekend in St. Louis, where the PGA Tour’s BMW Championship was being held. Schmitt played in the tournament’s pro-am alongside world No. 1 player Scottie Scheffler, who is fresh off a win in Memphis and is looking to make a run for another FedEx Cup title.

An Alabama jury on Thursday awarded $9.25 million in damages after finding that The New York Times defamed Kai Spears, a college basketball player at the University of Alabama, by incorrectly reporting that he was at the scene of a fatal shooting in Tuscaloosa. Three other basketball players from the school were present at the January 2023 shooting, and Spears’s attorney praised the judge’s ruling. The Times could still appeal the decision.

Jocks on the Hill: Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.)

Sen. Chris Coons, one of several Democrats working with Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) to get the Protect College Sports Act passed once lawmakers return from recess, answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“Football. I played in high school, my son-in-law and father-in-law played. I married into a Penn State-obsessed family. My father-in-law and brother-in-law made me take a quiz about Penn State football before I married my wife, and I flunked it cold. If it wasn’t for my now mother-in-law, I don’t think I would have made it. It’s something that’s bonded our family.”

“Our other son Jack went to Notre Dame, and we’ve become a big Notre Dame family. So in the fall, I’m watching Eagles, Notre Dame, Penn State pretty much every weekend, and my wife Annie is a huge football fan.”

Is there an athlete you looked up to growing up?

“The Flyers, Sixers and Phillies in the late ’70s, early ’80s. … I was pretty focused on high school sports, though. The Phillies won the World Series when I was a junior in high school, and Dallas Green’s son was a classmate of mine, so we followed him pretty closely.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you love to root against?

“Ohio State, for sure. Sometimes Michigan. The Commanders, I almost said the Redskins, and you know … Dallas, Dallas, Dallas.”
